summary:
## Building a Custom Fly Fishing Net from Koa Wood

This project details the process of creating a one-of-a-kind fly fishing landing net from highly figured Koa wood. The build involves steam bending, lamination, detailed shaping, and finishing techniques.

## Frame Construction

Key steps for building the net's frame:

*   **Steam Bending**: Thin strips of Koa wood are steamed for 15 minutes to make them pliable. They are then immediately placed into a form to dry and take the shape of the net hoop.
*   **Lamination & Glue-Up**: Once shaped, the strips are laminated together inside the form using **Gorilla Glue** to create a strong, solid frame. The handle is cut on a bandsaw and integrated into the glue-up.
*   **Shaping**: After the glue cures, the frame is removed from the mold. The shape is refined using a **bandsaw**, a **drum sander** to flatten the faces, a **router** for edge profiles, and extensive hand sanding.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> Koa wood can be prone to **checking** (cracking) during steam bending. An effective field repair is to quickly apply Gorilla Glue into the cracks and clamp them shut while the wood is still warm.

## Net Channel & Mounting

Final details are added to the frame to prepare for mounting the net basket.

*   **Routing the Net Channel**: A channel is routed along the inside edge of the hoop to hold the net's attachment string. 

> [!NOTE]
> To make an improvised depth adjustment on a router bit, electrical tape was carefully wrapped around the bearing to pack it out, reducing the cut depth from an excessive 3/16" to a more suitable 1/8".

*   **Drilling the Hole Pattern**: A specific pattern is crucial for even net support. The pattern used here consists of:
    *   Two holes spaced **1/2 inch** apart (center-to-center).
    *   A **1.5 to 2 inch** space before the next pair of holes.
    *   This pattern is repeated all around the hoop.

> [!TIP]
> Use a **Dremel** with a ball-end tool to slightly countersink each drill hole from the inside. This removes rough edges and prevents the attachment line from catching or fraying.

## Finishing & Final Assembly

*   **Finish Coat**: The net received **seven coats of clear glossy urethane**. Between each coat, the surface was lightly sanded with **400 grit sandpaper and steel wool** to achieve a smooth, durable, and waterproof finish.
*   **Assembly**: The final step is to sew the silicone catch-and-release net basket into the frame using the drilled holes and the routed channel.

## Drilling Holes for the Net Basket

Whoops. Well, sometimes life gets a little bit rushed and you accidentally erase the super, super beautiful footage showing your priceless net being drilled for mounting the net basket. Whoopsy. Luckily, once you build a few nets, it kind of becomes a bit of an addiction and you have a few just hanging around. So I'm going to use this oak and walnut net to walk you through the drilling pattern I use for ensuring a good support of the silicone catch-and-release net that I'll be actually putting in the Koa one shortly. Oh, and I'll put a link to the net I use down in the description. It's important to remember that there's a ton of nets out there and they'll all mount a little bit differently. The key is ensuring that there's an even tie-in where there's no sagging or stretch of the silicone, or as little as possible. 

Hole placement isn't really complex. You just need a slightly oversized bit, sharp pencil, a tape measure, and the actual net you plan to use on hand. A small clamp or two can also be very handy to get the best results. Basically on this style of net basket, I'm taking two holes that are spaced center to center 1/2 inch apart followed by a one and a half inch space, then repeated that all the way around. Now that's with this size of net right here. On the Koa and the oak and walnut net will actually be two inches spacing between half inch sections. I like to drill several sections of holes, check the rough fit, and then keep going until I reach the end of the string channel on the opposite side. 

And when you're done drilling you get some bonus points if you take a Dremel with a ball end tool and kind of countersink the holes, each hole inside mount, to get rid of any rough spots where the D-line might catch. And after that, a bit more sanding and then it's on to finish, which I also conveniently lost.
